These findings establish a physical basis for depth-resolved modification in laser nanomanufacturing, providing a dual-capacity for simultaneous surface patterning and depth-resolved subsurface modification with direct applications in laser-assisted interfacial separation and 3D integrated photonic fabrication.

AI.tldr: Femtosecond-laser energy deposition in silicon-on-insulator thin films is governed by carrier-induced refractive-index modulation coupled with self-induced Fabry-Pérot resonances, yielding three excitation regimes and a nonlinear hotspot migration effect; at high fluence, plasma shielding replaces resonance-mediated absorption.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to clarify how spatial energy distribution in silicon thin films under femtosecond laser irradiation can be understood and controlled, thereby supporting depth-resolved modification for laser nanomanufacturing.
AI.method: The authors analyze silicon-on-insulator configurations with thicknesses of 100, 230, and 350 nm, using numerical modeling to examine the interaction between carrier-induced refractive-index modulation and self-induced Fabry-Pérot resonances.
AI.result: Three characteristic excitation regions are resolved: interface-localized, binodal, and multi-nodal regimes. A nonlinear hotspot migration effect is reported in which transient refractive-index reduction stretches the internal standing wave and moves intensity antinodes toward the film volume during the pulse. At higher fluences, plasma-induced extinction suppresses internal reflections, causing a transition from resonance-mediated absorption to plasma shielding.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a physical basis for depth-resolved modification in laser nanomanufacturing, enabling simultaneous surface patterning and depth-resolved subsurface modification, with applications in laser-assisted interfacial separation and 3D integrated photonic fabrication.

title: Reinforcement Learning Controllers for Fusion Scenario Development
summary: Scenario development, the design of the waveforms that take a tokamak discharge from breakdown to flat-top, is still an iterative, labour-intensive process. Every candidate scenario has to be simulated with a controller in the loop, and the classical shape and current controllers need low-level actuator references. So the process is iterative and includes a number of trial-and-error steps. We propose to replace the per-scenario controller tuning by a single goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning controller trained once, in advance, against a free-boundary equilibrium and transport simulator. A scenario is then specified only by the target waveforms of the physical quantities of interest (plasma current, line-averaged electron density, LCFS shape, x-point positions), and the controller produces the coil-current and fueling commands that realize them. We demonstrate the approach on an EAST plasma-current ramp-up: the controller takes over a small limited plasma, ramps the current and the density, grows the cross-section, forms two x-points and holds a double-null diverted configuration against sampled shape targets for the rest of a 1.2 s episode. The neural network controller is trained using TQC algorithm. On 1024 test scenarios sampled from a low-discrepancy scrambled Sobol sequence in 11-dimensional target space, the controller forms the divertor in 86% of the cases, holds it for more than 0.5 s in 67% and reaches the end of the episode in a diverted state in 58%, with flat-top tracking errors of a few kA in plasma current, $\sim 0.15\times10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in density, $\sim 2$ cm in position and $\sim 8$ cm in x-point location; the failures concentrate at the high-current density ($J$) region which is believed to be physically or from engineering perspective not feasible within ohmic mode.

AI.tldr: A single goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning controller, trained once with TQC against a free-boundary equilibrium and transport simulator, replaces iterative per-scenario controller tuning and is demonstrated on an EAST plasma-current ramp-up with quantified divertor formation and tracking performance.
AI.motivation: Tokamak scenario development is iterative and labour-intensive: each candidate scenario must be simulated with a controller in the loop, and classical shape and current controllers require low-level actuator references, leading to repeated trial-and-error tuning.
AI.method: The authors train one goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning controller in advance using the TQC algorithm against a free-boundary equilibrium and transport simulator. A scenario is specified only by target waveforms for plasma current, line-averaged electron density, LCFS shape, and x-point positions; the controller outputs coil-current and fueling commands. The approach is demonstrated on an EAST plasma-current ramp-up from a small limited plasma to a double-null diverted configuration over a 1.2 s episode.
AI.result: On 1024 test scenarios sampled from a low-discrepancy scrambled Sobol sequence in an 11-dimensional target space, the controller formed the divertor in 86% of cases, held it for more than 0.5 s in 67%, and reached the end of the episode in a diverted state in 58%. Flat-top tracking errors were a few kA in plasma current, about 0.15 x 10^19 m^-3 in density, about 2 cm in position, and about 8 cm in x-point location. Failures concentrate in the high-current-density region, believed not feasible in ohmic mode from physical or engineering perspectives.
AI.conclusion: The results support replacing per-scenario controller tuning with a single pre-trained goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning controller that maps target waveforms to coil-current and fueling commands, while indicating that failures at high current density may reflect physical or engineering infeasibility within ohmic mode.

title: A Unified Interface Neural Network for Elliptic Interface Problems
summary: We develop a Unified Interface Neural Network (UINN) framework for elliptic interface problems with discontinuous coefficients. A single shared network provides a unified representation of the solution in both subdomains, while a projection--correction construction embeds the solution and flux jump conditions directly into the neural trial space. This design aligns with the classical numerical principle of incorporating interfacial physics into the approximation basis to construct interface-unfitted numerical methods. The jump conditions are therefore satisfied exactly for any network parameters. Compared with methods based on separate phase networks and numerical formulations with interface penalty terms, UINN provides a unified representation with exact enforcement of interfacial jump conditions and interface-penalty-free optimization. Those features streamline the numerical formulations and can enhance training robustness. Numerical experiments on smooth interfaces at modestly large and high coefficient contrasts demonstrate UINN's solution accuracy, near-machine-precision satisfaction of the interface jump conditions, and enhanced robustness.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Unified Interface Neural Network (UINN) framework for elliptic interface problems with discontinuous coefficients, using one shared network and a projection-correction construction to enforce solution and flux jump conditions exactly without interface penalties.
AI.motivation: Elliptic interface problems with discontinuous coefficients require numerical methods that handle interfacial physics and jump conditions. The authors aim to align neural network design with the classical principle of embedding interfacial physics into the approximation basis and to avoid separate phase networks and interface penalty terms.
AI.method: UINN uses a single shared network to represent the solution across both subdomains. A projection-correction construction embeds the solution and flux jump conditions directly into the neural trial space, yielding an interface-unfitted method in which jump conditions are satisfied exactly for any network parameters and optimization is interface-penalty-free.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on smooth interfaces with modestly large and high coefficient contrasts demonstrate solution accuracy, near-machine-precision satisfaction of interface jump conditions, and enhanced robustness.
AI.conclusion: UINN provides a unified representation with exact enforcement of interfacial jump conditions and interface-penalty-free optimization, streamlining numerical formulations and potentially enhancing training robustness compared with separate phase networks and interface-penalty formulations.

title: How stagnation lines move, persist and break up in fluid flows
summary: Stagnation curves of arbitrary shape (zeros of $\mathbf v(\mathbf x,t)$) are non-generic yet common; we derive their motion. Differentiating $\mathbf v=\mathbf0$ gives $\mathbf L\mathbf U=-\mathbf a$ ($\mathbf U$ curve velocity, $\mathbf a=\mathbf v_t$, $\mathbf L=\nabla\mathbf v$ kills tangent, acts on normal plane via $2\times2$ block $\mathbf K$); dynamics enters only via $\mathbf a$. Normal velocity: $-\mathbf K^{-1}$ times normal $\mathbf a$; tangential solvability: scalar condition $Σ=0$ per point ($Σ$: part of $\mathbf a$ outside range $\mathbf L$). Potential flow: $\mathbf K$ is strain rate, normal velocity pressure gradient over principal strain rate $ε$, persistence needs uniform pressure on it. Stokes flow: tangential vorticity enters $\mathbf K$ (centre lines), $Σ$ involves normal vorticity. Navier-Stokes: $Σ$ set by instantaneous flow via nonlocal pressure, viscosity. If $Σ\ne0$, line becomes, to first order in $t$, isolated points at zeros of $Σ$ (critical points of $\varphi_t$ if potential; maybe none in Stokes flow: loops vanish). Symmetry (line an orbit of rigid-motion group, no velocity along it) suffices for persistence, not necessary: flows steady in rigidly moving frame have $Σ\equiv0$. Incompressibility enters via $\mathrm{tr}\mathbf K=0$; for inviscid irrotational homentropic compressible flow, line dilatation is $\varphi_{tt}/c^2$, so lines can be nodes, persistence needs uniform enthalpy, singular $\mathbf K$ arises at ordinary points, acoustic standing waves give exact examples (node line breaking into alternating sinks, saddles); also degenerate $\mathbf K$ (pairs born at distance $O(\sqrt t)$), curvature, torsion evolution, closure for moving-singularity-driven flows, helical and elliptically conical stagnation-point flow, exact Navier-Stokes example: saddle, centre lines split into four points per period.

AI.tldr: The paper derives how stagnation curves—zeros of a velocity field with arbitrary shape—move and persist. Differentiating v=0 yields a linear system whose 2×2 normal block K controls normal motion and whose tangential solvability condition Σ=0 controls persistence; the framework is applied to potential, Stokes, Navier–Stokes, incompressible and compressible flows and illustrated by exact examples.
AI.motivation: Stagnation curves of arbitrary shape are non-generic yet common, so the paper aims to explain their motion, persistence and breakup rather than treating them as exceptional. The abstract does not provide further application-specific motivation.
AI.method: Differentiate v=0 to obtain L U = −a, where U is curve velocity, a=v_t and L=∇v. L kills the tangent and acts on the normal plane through a 2×2 block K; dynamics enter only through a. The normal velocity is −K^{-1} times the normal component of a, while tangential solvability requires the scalar condition Σ=0 at each point, where Σ is the part of a outside the range of L. The analysis specializes this condition to potential flow, Stokes flow and Navier–Stokes flow, uses tr K=0 for incompressibility, and examines compressible inviscid irrotational homentropic flow, degenerate K, curvature and torsion evolution, and exact example flows.
AI.result: In potential flow K is the strain-rate tensor; the normal velocity is the pressure gradient divided by the principal strain rate ε, and persistence requires uniform pressure on the line. In Stokes flow tangential vorticity enters K for centre lines and Σ involves normal vorticity. In Navier–Stokes flow Σ is set instantaneously by the flow through nonlocal pressure and viscosity. If Σ≠0, to first order in t the line becomes isolated points at zeros of Σ—critical points of φ_t in potential flow—and in Stokes flow there may be none, so loops vanish. Symmetry suffices for persistence but is not necessary; flows steady in a rigidly moving frame have Σ≡0. Incompressibility gives tr K=0; for inviscid irrotational homentropic compressible flow the line dilatation is φ_tt/c^2, so lines can be nodes, persistence requires uniform enthalpy, singular K arises at ordinary points, and acoustic standing waves give exact examples in which a node line breaks into alternating sinks and saddles. Degenerate K produces pairs born at distance O(√t); curvature, torsion evolution, closure for moving-singularity-driven flows, helical and elliptically conical stagnation-point flow are also treated. An exact Navier–Stokes example shows a saddle and centre lines splitting into four points per period.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that stagnation-curve motion and persistence are governed by the normal block K and the scalar solvability condition Σ, with the surrounding flow entering through a and, in Navier–Stokes, through nonlocal pressure and viscosity. It provides a general classification of persistence versus breakup and exact examples across several flow classes; no quantitative experimental validation is reported in the abstract.

title: Superradiant temporal transition radiation of a relativistic electron beam
summary: A charge in uniform motion carries a bound field that does not radiate. Transition radiation releases part of it at a boundary in space. We propose and analyze the case of radiation emission due to a boundary in time: a relativistic electron bunch passes through an aperture in a semiconductor (silicon) wafer, and while its bound field occupies the wafer, a femtosecond laser switches the semiconductor into an electron-hole plasma. The field is a valid solution of the old medium and not of the new one, so it is handed to the plasma as an initial condition for radiation emission at the plasma frequency. Because in temporal transition radiation (t-TR) the wavevector is conserved, and the frequency is not, the emission can appear in a spectral band that the bunch's own field does not populate. Every electron contributes in phase to the initial condition at the switching moment, so the emitted energy scales as $N^2$. We derive the field energy conversion at the temporal boundary and the resultant measurable amplitude and frequency line-shape of the radiation taking into consideration plasma carriers collisional loss. The simplified analytical model of the process and its scaling laws are confirmed by use of FDTD numerical computations for a reference case based on the parameters of an existing 6.5 MeV photoinjector accelerator. For this case we predict wideband t-TR radiation emission at THz frequencies, where the emission center frequency, near the plasma frequency, is selectable across an octave, set by the laser fluence, and the intensity is governed by the beam charge. The predicted radiative energy is detectable in a single shot. The experimental considerations for observing it are given in a Supplement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and analyzes temporal transition radiation (t-TR): a relativistic electron bunch passes through an aperture in a silicon wafer, and a femtosecond laser switches the wafer into an electron-hole plasma, causing the bunch's bound field to be released as radiation because the field is valid in the old medium but not the new one. An analytical model including collisional plasma loss is validated by FDTD simulations using an existing 6.5 MeV photoinjector reference case, predicting single-shot-detectable, laser-fluence-tunable wideband THz emission with N^2 scaling.
AI.motivation: A uniformly moving charge carries a nonradiating bound field that can be released at a spatial boundary via transition radiation. The paper motivates an analogous boundary in time, where a fast medium-switching event converts the bound field into radiation and enables emission in spectral bands not populated by the bunch's own field.
AI.method: The authors propose a relativistic electron bunch passing through an aperture in a semiconductor (silicon) wafer while its bound field occupies the wafer; a femtosecond laser switches the semiconductor into an electron-hole plasma. They derive the field-energy conversion at the temporal boundary and the measurable amplitude and frequency line shape, including plasma-carrier collisional loss. A simplified analytical model and its scaling laws are checked against FDTD numerical computations for a reference case based on an existing 6.5 MeV photoinjector accelerator.
AI.result: The analytical scaling laws are confirmed by FDTD computations. For the reference case, the authors predict wideband t-TR emission at THz frequencies, with center frequency near the plasma frequency selectable across an octave via laser fluence and intensity governed by beam charge. Every electron contributes in phase at the switching moment, so emitted energy scales as N^2. The predicted radiative energy is detectable in a single shot. Numerical energy values and full experimental details are not provided in the abstract; experimental considerations are stated to be in a Supplement.
AI.conclusion: Temporal transition radiation from laser-induced plasma switching is predicted to provide a tunable, wideband THz source whose emission frequency is set by laser fluence and whose intensity is controlled by beam charge, with N^2 coherent scaling and single-shot detectability. The authors conclude that the process is supported by analytical modeling and FDTD validation and provide experimental considerations for observing it in a Supplement.

title: Beyond Radiation Hydrodynamics: A Coupled Kinetic Plasma and Radiation Modeling of NIF Polar Direct Drive Capsule
summary: Predictive modeling of inertial-confinement-fusion (ICF) implosions increasingly requires resolving ion-kinetic effects beyond the reach of radiation-hydrodynamics, without sacrificing radiation transport. We present, to our knowledge, the first coupling of a kinetic-ion plasma model to thermal radiation transport. The iFP code - a conservative, spherically symmetric, 1D2V hybrid kinetic-ion/fluid-electron Vlasov-Fokker-Planck solver - is extended with a grey P1 radiation model, coupled through a high-order/low-order (HOLO) fixed-point solver and advanced on a shared adaptive moving mesh. Opacities are mixed on the fly from the LANL TOPS library, exploiting the per-species information intrinsic to a kinetic code. We verify the implementation against the optically thick Marshak-wave and Mach-45 radiative-shock benchmarks, and apply it to a NIF polar-direct-drive exploding-pusher capsule. Increasing physics fidelity systematically improves agreement with the measured neutron yield and burn width; the improvement is driven by kinetically enhanced fuel leakage and ballistic preheating, and radiation transport proves essential for quantitative agreement. This work establishes a proof-of-principle capability for higher-fidelity kinetic-plasma/radiation modeling of ICF.

AI.tldr: The authors report the first coupling of a kinetic-ion plasma model to thermal radiation transport, implemented in the iFP solver, verified on radiative benchmarks, and applied to a NIF exploding-pusher capsule, where higher physics fidelity improved agreement with measured neutron yield and burn width.
AI.motivation: Predictive modeling of inertial-confinement-fusion implosions increasingly requires ion-kinetic effects beyond radiation-hydrodynamics while retaining radiation transport; the abstract states that such a coupled kinetic-ion/radiation capability was previously lacking.
AI.method: The conservative, spherically symmetric, 1D2V hybrid kinetic-ion/fluid-electron Vlasov-Fokker-Planck iFP code was extended with a grey P1 radiation model, coupled via a high-order/low-order fixed-point solver and advanced on a shared adaptive moving mesh. Opacities are mixed on the fly from the LANL TOPS library using per-species kinetic information. The implementation was verified against the optically thick Marshak-wave and Mach-45 radiative-shock benchmarks and applied to a NIF polar-direct-drive exploding-pusher capsule.
AI.result: The implementation was verified against the Marshak-wave and Mach-45 radiative-shock benchmarks. For the NIF exploding-pusher capsule, increasing physics fidelity systematically improved agreement with measured neutron yield and burn width; the improvement was driven by kinetically enhanced fuel leakage and ballistic preheating, and radiation transport was essential for quantitative agreement. Numerical values are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a proof-of-principle capability for higher-fidelity kinetic-plasma/radiation modeling of inertial-confinement-fusion implosions.

title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement
summary: Bone scaffolds must reconcile a macroscale mechanical response with microscale geometric feasibility, yet conventional approaches to their design restrict attainable constitutive properties. This work presents a concurrent two-scale topology optimization framework; a conditional rectified flow generates periodic lattice microstructures, which are then refined in latent space by exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities. The resulting unit-cell geometries and their spatial assignments are jointly optimized under mechanical and feature-size constraints. In a distal rabbit femur benchmark, all eight flow-started refinements produce printable cells with maximum relative errors under 1\% across six prescribed engineering moduli. Constructing the implant from a single tiled cell reproduces intact whole-femur compliance within 0.1\% and regional strain energy within 0.35\% under four loading conditions. In human femoral reconstruction, multiscale concurrent optimization produces a cortical mid-shaft scaffold with porosity 63\% while satisfying the compliance constraint within 2\% under walking and stair-climbing loads. It achieves an 84\% porosity on a proximal cancellous scaffold with strain-energy deviations below 0.25\% under the same loads. Analysis of the learned representations reveals distinct architectural families in latent space. Further, the attention heads of the rectified-flow transformer specialize for spatial shifts -- learning the analogue of a finite-difference stencil -- and coordinate symmetries, with ablations showing their influence on generated topologies. These results establish a route to printable, mechanically constrained scaffold designs. The framework is general enough for extending to many other multiscale structural design applications including topology-microstructure co-design in metal additive manufacturing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a concurrent two-scale topology optimization framework that uses a conditional rectified flow and latent-space finite-element homogenization refinement to jointly design printable lattice microstructures and their spatial assignment for mechanically constrained bone scaffolds.
AI.motivation: Bone scaffolds must reconcile macroscale mechanical response with microscale geometric feasibility, but conventional design approaches restrict the attainable constitutive properties.
AI.method: A conditional rectified flow generates periodic lattice microstructures, which are refined in latent space using exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities. Unit-cell geometries and their spatial assignments are jointly optimized under mechanical and feature-size constraints.
AI.result: In a distal rabbit femur benchmark, all eight flow-started refinements produced printable cells with maximum relative errors under 1% across six prescribed engineering moduli. A single tiled cell reproduced intact whole-femur compliance within 0.1% and regional strain energy within 0.35% under four loading conditions. In human femoral reconstruction, multiscale concurrent optimization produced a cortical mid-shaft scaffold with 63% porosity while satisfying the compliance constraint within 2% under walking and stair-climbing loads, and achieved 84% porosity on a proximal cancellous scaffold with strain-energy deviations below 0.25% under the same loads. Learned representations showed distinct architectural families, and rectified-flow transformer attention heads specialized for spatial shifts and coordinate symmetries, with ablations showing their influence on generated topologies.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a route to printable, mechanically constrained scaffold designs, and the framework is general enough to extend to other multiscale structural design applications, including topology-microstructure co-design in metal additive manufacturing.

title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows
summary: This work presents the development and assessment of a hybrid framework coupling numerical simulation, experimental samples, data assimilation (DA) and machine learning (ML) to investigate the flow within an axial compressor stage. The methodology first implements a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter (MFEnKF) which integrates experimental PIV data with a two-fidelity numerical simulation setup, combining steady-state RANS on a fixed grid with unsteady hybrid RANS/LES simulations on a moving grid. This data assimilation step successfully reduces discrepancies between experiments and CFD realizations. Besides, it provides additional high fidelity samples when compared with the available PIV data. This enriched database is used to train machine learning (ML) tools, with the objective to obtain black-box forcing terms to be included in the discretized form of the Navier-Stokes equations. These models are expected to preserve the accuracy of the DA results while not longer requiring the input of experimental data. The neural network architecture used here maps local physical features such as the velocity, the velocity gradients and the turbulent viscosity, to obtain the volume forcing terms. The analysis of the performance of such ML models shows that global accuracy is preserved but localized increased errors in specific regions of the compressor, such as close to the blade tips, can exceed those observed from the baseline RANS simulations. To resolve this issue, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) method is employed, which classifies and combines the trained ML tools for different flow regions. The discrepancy with experimental data of this method is systematically lower than the one observed for the baseline RANS solution and very similar to the one obtained with the MFEnKF.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and assesses a hybrid framework combining PIV, multi-fidelity CFD, Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filtering, machine learning, and Mixture of Experts to model flow in an axial compressor stage. The MFEnKF reduces experiment-CFD discrepancies and enriches the training database; ML models learn volume forcing terms, and MoE classification improves regional accuracy, achieving discrepancies lower than baseline RANS and similar to MFEnKF.
AI.motivation: The work aims to investigate the flow within an axial compressor stage and to obtain machine-learning-based black-box forcing terms that preserve the accuracy of data-assimilation results while no longer requiring experimental data as input.
AI.method: The methodology implements a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter that integrates experimental PIV data with a two-fidelity numerical setup: steady-state RANS on a fixed grid and unsteady hybrid RANS/LES on a moving grid. The enriched database is used to train neural networks that map local features—velocity, velocity gradients, and turbulent viscosity—to volume forcing terms in the discretized Navier-Stokes equations. A Mixture of Experts method then classifies and combines the trained ML tools for different flow regions.
AI.result: The MFEnKF reduces discrepancies between experiments and CFD realizations and provides additional high-fidelity samples beyond the available PIV data. The ML models preserve global accuracy, but localized errors in regions such as near blade tips can exceed those of baseline RANS. The Mixture of Experts method yields discrepancies with experimental data that are systematically lower than baseline RANS and very similar to those obtained with the MFEnKF.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid data-assimilation and machine-learning framework, with Mixture of Experts regional classification, can reproduce MFEnKF-level agreement with experimental data while avoiding the need for experimental input during ML deployment, and it outperforms the baseline RANS solution in terms of discrepancy.

title: Design and synthesis of laser inscribed flexible Bragg gratings containing silicon oxynitride-doped silicon thin film for authentication applications with the insights from X-Ray Absorption Spectroscopy and Quantum Mechanical Calculations
summary: Silicon-on-insulator is mostly the main driving material system for the field of silicon photonics, including PICs, due to high index contrast and compatibility with current semiconductor manufacturing processes [1]. A recent example is silicon oxynitride-doped silicon [2] discovered recently by our group, offering to set a new position for the fields of silicon photonics with a precise control of refractive index from 2.1 to 2.5 together with the photosensitivity property at different wavelengths. In this study, we demonstrate that the synthesis of silicon oxynitride-doped silicon can be performed on a flexible substrate for the fabrication of Bragg gratings (BG) at low temperatures below 100 degrees Celsius that are emerging for advanced applications. Their use in preserving ultra-fast lasers inscribed micro-information has been demonstrated numerically and experimentally due to its multispectral reflection behaviour from the ultraviolet (UV) to the near-infrared (NIR) regions. The unique structural characteristics of silicon oxynitride-doped silicon were studied at the Si L, O K and N K edges using soft X-ray absorption studies. The quantum mechanical calculations provide the potential formation mechanism of SiON-doped Si, whereas the crystal structure prediction for bulk Si3N4-xOx was conducted using the particle swarm optimization method in combination with density functional theory (DFT).

AI.tldr: Silicon oxynitride-doped silicon was synthesized on a flexible substrate at temperatures below 100 °C and used to fabricate Bragg gratings that exhibit multispectral reflection from UV to NIR, enabling numerical and experimental preservation of ultrafast-laser-inscribed micro-information; soft X-ray absorption and DFT/particle-swarm calculations probed structure and formation mechanism.
AI.motivation: Silicon-on-insulator is the main material system for silicon photonics, including PICs, owing to its high index contrast and compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Silicon oxynitride-doped silicon was recently discovered by the authors’ group, offering precise refractive-index control from 2.1 to 2.5 and photosensitivity at different wavelengths, motivating low-temperature fabrication on flexible substrates for advanced applications.
AI.method: The authors synthesized silicon oxynitride-doped silicon on a flexible substrate at temperatures below 100 °C and fabricated Bragg gratings. They demonstrated preservation of ultrafast-laser-inscribed micro-information numerically and experimentally through multispectral reflection from UV to NIR. Structural characteristics were studied by soft X-ray absorption at the Si L, O K, and N K edges. Quantum mechanical calculations addressed the potential formation mechanism of SiON-doped Si, and crystal structure prediction for bulk Si3N4-xOx used particle swarm optimization combined with DFT.
AI.result: Bragg gratings were fabricated from silicon oxynitride-doped silicon on a flexible substrate at low temperature. The structures showed multispectral reflection from UV to NIR, and their use in preserving ultrafast-laser-inscribed micro-information was demonstrated numerically and experimentally. Soft X-ray absorption revealed structural characteristics at the Si L, O K, and N K edges, while calculations provided a potential formation mechanism and a predicted crystal structure for bulk Si3N4-xOx. Quantitative grating performance metrics are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Silicon oxynitride-doped silicon can be synthesized on flexible substrates below 100 °C and used for Bragg gratings that preserve ultrafast-laser-inscribed micro-information via multispectral UV–NIR reflection. Combined soft X-ray absorption, quantum mechanical calculations, and DFT-based crystal structure prediction support understanding of its structure and formation mechanism. Specific performance limits and application-scale results are not provided in the abstract.

title: Ion Heating in Pair-loaded Relativistic Turbulence
summary: Pair-loaded relativistic turbulence is expected in compact high-energy astrophysical environments and may sustain plasma heating. Using self-consistent three-dimensional radiative particle-in-cell simulations, we identify the mechanism of ion heating mediated by pair-enhanced radiative feedback in relativistic turbulence. We derive the theoretical criterion for the transition to a regime dominated by radiative feedback and show that pair loading promotes the growth and persistence of large, connected optically thick structures. These long-lived structures sustain intense localized ion heating, repeatedly generating prominent hot-ion clumps and substantially enhancing the mean ion temperature. Our results establish a physical link between pair creation and sustained ion heating, providing a theoretical basis for investigating intermittent hot-ion production in black-hole coronae and gamma-ray burst outflows.

AI.tldr: Self-consistent 3D radiative particle-in-cell simulations show that pair-enhanced radiative feedback in relativistic turbulence creates long-lived optically thick structures that repeatedly produce hot-ion clumps and raise mean ion temperature.
AI.motivation: Pair-loaded relativistic turbulence is expected in compact high-energy astrophysical environments and may sustain plasma heating; the paper aims to establish a physical link between pair creation and sustained ion heating.
AI.method: The authors use self-consistent three-dimensional radiative particle-in-cell simulations, derive a theoretical criterion for transition to a radiative-feedback-dominated regime, and examine how pair loading affects the growth and persistence of large, connected optically thick structures.
AI.result: The simulations identify ion heating mediated by pair-enhanced radiative feedback. Pair loading promotes the growth and persistence of large, connected optically thick structures; these long-lived structures sustain intense localized ion heating, repeatedly generate prominent hot-ion clumps, and substantially enhance the mean ion temperature.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a physical link between pair creation and sustained ion heating and provide a theoretical basis for investigating intermittent hot-ion production in black-hole coronae and gamma-ray burst outflows.

title: Decoherence of the pair entangled states at thermalization and interparticle interaction. Heisenberg--Wigner path integral Monte Carlo simulations
summary: For deeper understanding of quantum non-local correlations a new path integral real-time quantum dynamics approach has been developed and applied to the Monte Carlo simulation of the decoherence of pair entangled states in many-body systems in the framework of the ``replica trick''. Calculations have been carried out for the Heisenberg-Wigner path integral representation of the entangled state correlation function (ESCF) in the modified unified electron gas model as example. The Wiener-Khinchin transformation of ESCF has been applied to random paths in path integral allowing for the Monte Carlo simulation of ESCF. Presented results include the spin-resolved radial distribution functions, ESCFs and estimations of the decoherence time of the entangled electron pairs due to thermalization and interparticle interaction.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a real-time path-integral quantum-dynamics approach, combined with the replica trick and Monte Carlo simulation, to study decoherence of pair-entangled states in many-body systems and demonstrates it on a modified unified electron gas model.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to gain deeper understanding of quantum non-local correlations by developing a new approach for simulating the decoherence of pair-entangled states in many-body systems.
AI.method: The authors use a real-time path-integral quantum-dynamics approach with the replica trick and Monte Carlo simulation. They calculate the Heisenberg-Wigner path-integral representation of the entangled state correlation function (ESCF) in the modified unified electron gas model, applying the Wiener-Khinchin transformation of the ESCF to random paths in the path integral.
AI.result: The presented results include spin-resolved radial distribution functions, ESCFs, and estimates of the decoherence time of entangled electron pairs due to thermalization and interparticle interaction.
AI.conclusion: The developed approach enables Monte Carlo simulation of the ESCF and estimation of decoherence times for entangled pairs in many-body systems, as demonstrated for the modified unified electron gas model; the abstract does not provide broader conclusions.

title: Bridging the Lattice Boltzmann Method and Moment Methods
summary: We derive discrete moment equations exactly equivalent to the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) and identify the general moment closure shared by kinetic methods based on the discrete-velocity Boltzmann equation. This closure provides a route to correct lower-order dynamics without requiring accurate reconstruction of the higher-order moments, thereby substantially broadening the scope of existing closure strategies that seek increasingly accurate representations of these moments. These advances establish a unified moment framework bridging LBM and moment methods. The framework enables efficient simulations across all Knudsen regimes, overcoming the prohibitive complexity of existing moment methods at high Knudsen numbers. It further provides a common basis for integrating and extending key features of diverse kinetic methods.

AI.tldr: The paper derives discrete moment equations exactly equivalent to the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM), identifies a general moment closure for discrete-velocity kinetic methods, and establishes a unified moment framework for efficient simulations across all Knudsen regimes.
AI.motivation: Existing closure strategies seek increasingly accurate representations of higher-order moments, while existing moment methods face prohibitive complexity at high Knudsen numbers. The paper aims to correct lower-order dynamics without accurate higher-order moment reconstruction and to bridge LBM and moment methods.
AI.method: The authors derive discrete moment equations exactly equivalent to LBM and identify a general moment closure shared by kinetic methods based on the discrete-velocity Boltzmann equation. The abstract does not provide algorithmic or numerical implementation details.
AI.result: The closure enables correction of lower-order dynamics without requiring accurate reconstruction of higher-order moments, broadening existing closure strategies. The framework enables efficient simulations across all Knudsen regimes and provides a common basis for integrating and extending key features of diverse kinetic methods. No quantitative results are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The advances establish a unified moment framework bridging LBM and moment methods, overcoming the prohibitive complexity of existing moment methods at high Knudsen numbers and providing a common basis for integrating and extending features of diverse kinetic methods.

title: All-Dielectric Tight-Binding Photonics via a Band-Gap Vacuum
summary: Tight-binding photonics bridges condensed-matter physics and optics, providing a powerful framework for engineering band structures and topological phases with light. For photons, however, the vacuum is gapless, so resonators in air carry radiative tails that produce spurious long-range couplings. Here we embed resonators in a photonic band-gap vacuum (BgV), a photonic crystal whose band gap plays for photons the role vacuum plays for bound electrons. The BgV localizes each resonance exponentially, so designed short-range couplings define the lattice Hamiltonian. We thereby experimentally realize a faithful Benalcazar-Bernevig-Hughes Hamiltonian in an all-dielectric photonic crystal, resolving corner resonances and their orbitals in microwave measurements. Unlike the vacuum surrounding electrons, the BgV is itself designable, controlling relative couplings and closed-loop interference through its band dispersion and Bloch modes. Full-wave calculations and extracted models show that uniformly modifying the BgV, with all resonators fixed, switches the quantized polarization of a two-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice and converts a zero-flux lattice into a $π$-flux one. We also numerically realize three-dimensional pyrochlore and hyperhoneycomb lattices with space groups $R\bar{3}m$ and $C2/c$, the latter a nodal-loop semimetal with topological drumhead surface states. These results establish the BgV as a designable vacuum for all-dielectric tight-binding photonics in two and three dimensions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a photonic band-gap vacuum (BgV) to suppress radiative long-range couplings between resonators, enabling faithful all-dielectric tight-binding photonic lattices. It experimentally realizes a BBH model in microwave measurements and shows that BgV design can switch SSH polarization and flux, while numerical models realize 3D pyrochlore and hyperhoneycomb lattices including a nodal-loop semimetal.
AI.motivation: Tight-binding photonics offers a framework for engineering band structures and topological phases with light, but photons in air experience a gapless vacuum, causing resonators to have radiative tails and spurious long-range couplings that spoil designed lattice Hamiltonians.
AI.method: Resonators are embedded in a photonic band-gap vacuum, a photonic crystal whose band gap plays the role of vacuum for bound electrons and exponentially localizes each resonance so that designed short-range couplings define the lattice Hamiltonian. The work uses an all-dielectric photonic crystal, microwave measurements, full-wave calculations, extracted models, and numerical realizations of three-dimensional lattices.
AI.result: The authors experimentally realize a faithful Benalcazar-Bernevig-Hughes Hamiltonian and resolve corner resonances and their orbitals in microwave measurements. They show that uniformly modifying the BgV while keeping all resonators fixed switches the quantized polarization of a two-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice and converts a zero-flux lattice into a pi-flux lattice. They also numerically realize three-dimensional pyrochlore and hyperhoneycomb lattices with space groups R-3m and C2/c, the latter being a nodal-loop semimetal with topological drumhead surface states.
AI.conclusion: The BgV is established as a designable vacuum for all-dielectric tight-binding photonics in two and three dimensions, with band dispersion and Bloch modes providing control over relative couplings and closed-loop interference.

title: A mixed leading variable physics-informed neural network for nonsmooth dynamics simulation in contact systems
summary: High-accuracy computation of nonsmooth dynamics is a challenging problem in systems with multiple frictional contacts. This study proposes a general physics-informed neural network framework, termed the mixed leading variable physics-informed neural network (MLV-PINN). By using the governing equations and contact-friction laws as physical constraints, this framework provides common solution approaches for computing nonsmooth dynamics not only in discrete systems but also in continuum systems. Specifically, the network represents accelerations, normal contact forces and friction margins as independent outputs and determines them simultaneously, without first reducing the dynamics to discrete velocity-impulse complementary subproblems. A composite physics-informed loss is constructed from the equations of motion in their original form, contact-friction complementary conditions and a friction-margin consistency relation. To improve stick-slip state identification during PINN optimisation, a mixed leading variable combining relative tangential velocity and acceleration is introduced to reformulate the tangential complementary conditions. Four benchmark simulations cover one-dimensional (1-D) nonsmooth dynamics involving single-contact stick-slip, 1-D nonsmooth dynamics involving multi-contact stick-slip, two-dimensional (2-D) nonsmooth dynamics with coupled normal contact-separation and tangential stick-slip, and 2-D nonsmooth dynamics in a continuum system involving moving contact on an elastic beam. Benchmark comparisons show substantial reductions in displacement and velocity errors relative to the corresponding conventional methods at large time steps. These results, together with an ablation study and tests involving friction-velocity slopes, long-time integration and loss weights, illustrate the computational accuracy and support the broad applicability of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MLV-PINN, a general physics-informed neural network framework for high-accuracy nonsmooth dynamics with frictional contacts. title: CuAD: Source-to-Source Automatic Differentiation of CUDA Kernels for Discrete Adjoints in Computational Fluid Dynamics
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Code available at https://github.com/SEUNGHYUN-JOO/CuAD
summary: Discrete adjoint methods give the sensitivities that aerodynamic design and data assimilation require, but they remain hard to obtain for flow solvers that run on graphics processors. This paper presents CuAD, a source-to-source automatic differentiation tool that reads CUDA kernels and writes their tangent and adjoint versions as ordinary CUDA source. Its reverse mode is organised around the GPU thread and exploits the structure of flow-solver kernels: pure accumulations need no tape, the remaining intermediate values are recomputed rather than stored, and adjoint updates are atomic only where several threads reach the same memory. We evaluate CuAD on four kernels from simple flow models: a viscous Burgers residual, a two-dimensional advection-diffusion residual, a quasi-one-dimensional Euler residual and a Biot-Savart summation over point vortices. All generated derivatives agree with finite differences and pass adjoint dot-product tests to round-off, while the adjoint kernels cost two to six times the primal kernels. Compared with the compiler-based tool Clad under the same compiler, CuAD gives identical results at identical cost on the stencil kernels and is 16 to 470 times faster on the summation kernel because it stores no tape. A steady Burgers study shows that in single precision the adjoint gradient of a finite-difference Jacobian reaches errors of 45 to 75 per cent once the condition number grows to $2.5\times10^{5}$, whereas the CuAD Jacobian keeps the error below $5\times10^{-5}$. Four applications complete the evaluation: adjoint fields of the Burgers shock, the sensitivity of a scalar sensor in a cellular vortex, the inverse design of a transonic nozzle whose area is recovered to $2\times10^{-8}$, and an unsteady adjoint of the roll-up of a vortex sheet over 400 time steps.

title: High-Efficiency Silicon-Lithium Niobate Grating Coupler enabled by Fully-Etched Subwavelength Structures
summary: A new approach of silicon-lithium niobate (Si-LN) grating couplers (GCs) with a fully-etched structure is proposed. The coupling strength is engineered through subwavelength structures, allowing improved directionality. The adjoint-based inverse design method is simultaneously adopted to achieve efficient coupling between photonic circuits and fibers. Considering the birefringence of LN, the proposed Si-LN GCs are optimized and fabricated for TE mode along the crystallographic Z and Y directions. The experimentally measured coupling efficiencies are -3.3 dB and -3.9 dB along the crystallographic Z and Y directions, respectively. The measured 3-dB bandwidths are broader than 54 nm and the back reflections can be suppressed down to -15 dB over 50 nm for both directions. The proposed Si-LN GCs are realized by only single-step Si etching, offering a practical solution for fast device prototyping in Si-LN photonic integrated circuits.

AI.motivation: The work aims to achieve efficient coupling between photonic circuits and fibers in silicon-lithium niobate photonic integrated circuits while offering a practical route for fast device prototyping through single-step silicon etching.

Adjoint-based inverse design is used for efficient fiber-to-circuit coupling. Accounting for lithium niobate birefringence, devices are optimized and fabricated for TE mode along the crystallographic Z and Y directions using only single-step silicon etching.

title: Magneto-Rayleigh-Taylor instability driven by a rotating magnetic field: Cylindrical liner configuration
summary: We propose using a directional time-varying (rotating) driving magnetic field to suppress magneto-Rayleigh-Taylor (MRT) instability in dynamic Z-pinches. A rotational drive magnetic field is equivalent to two magnetic-field components, Θ and Z, that alternate in time, referred to as an alternate Theta-Z-pinch configuration. We consider the finitely thick cylindrical liner configuration in this paper. We numerically integrate the perturbation equation to stagnation time based on the optimal background unperturbed trajectories. We assess the cumulative growth of the dominant mode selected by some mechanism at the beginning of an implosion. The maximum e-folding number at stagnation of the dominant mode of an optimized alternate Theta-Z-pinch is significantly lower than that of the standard Theta- or Z-pinch. The directional rotation of the magnetic field contributes to suppress the instabilities, independent of the finite thickness. The finite thickness effect plays a role only when the orientation of the magnetic field varies in time whereas it does not appear in the standard Theta- or Z-pinch. The rotating frequency of the magnetic field and the thickness of liner are both having a monotonic effect on suppression. Their synergistic effect can enhance the suppression on MRT instability. Because the MRT instability can be well suppressed in this way, the alternate Theta-Z-pinch configuration has potential applications in liner inertial fusion. This work is supported by the NSFC (Grant Nos. 11405167, 51407171, 11571293, 11605188, and 11605189) and the Foundation of the China Academy of Engineering Physics (No. 2015B0201023).

AI.tldr: A rotating, time-varying driving magnetic field is proposed to suppress magneto-Rayleigh-Taylor instability in dynamic Z-pinches by alternating Theta and Z magnetic-field components; numerical perturbation-growth analysis shows significantly reduced growth at stagnation versus standard Theta- or Z-pinches.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to suppress magneto-Rayleigh-Taylor (MRT) instability in dynamic Z-pinches, with potential application to liner inertial fusion.
AI.method: The authors propose an alternate Theta-Z-pinch configuration driven by a directional time-varying rotating magnetic field, equivalent to two alternating Theta and Z components. They consider a finitely thick cylindrical liner and numerically integrate the perturbation equation to stagnation time using optimal background unperturbed trajectories, assessing cumulative growth of the dominant mode selected at the beginning of implosion.
AI.result: The maximum e-folding number at stagnation for the dominant mode of an optimized alternate Theta-Z-pinch is significantly lower than for the standard Theta- or Z-pinch. Magnetic-field rotation suppresses instabilities independently of finite thickness; finite thickness affects suppression only when the magnetic-field orientation varies in time. Rotating frequency and liner thickness both have monotonic suppression effects, and their synergy can enhance MRT suppression.
AI.conclusion: The alternate Theta-Z-pinch configuration can substantially suppress MRT instability and therefore has potential applications in liner inertial fusion.

title: LIDAR with Optically Amplified Thermal Light
summary: Thermal light exhibits intensity fluctuations or photon bunching that has been used as a source of entropy or temporally correlated light. However, its low spectral density limits its use in practical applications like LIDAR. One method of remedying this is optical amplification to boost its brightness. In this paper, we show that the normalized second order coherence function $g^{(2)}(τ)$ of a thermal light source is preserved after amplification. We then use amplified thermal light to demonstrate a LIDAR raster scan of a building at 1.3 km with a depth resolution of 2 cm.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that optical amplification preserves the normalized second-order coherence function of thermal light and uses amplified thermal light to perform a 1.3 km LIDAR raster scan of a building with 2 cm depth resolution.
AI.motivation: Thermal light has intensity fluctuations and photon bunching useful as an entropy source or temporally correlated light, but its low spectral density limits practical applications such as LIDAR; optical amplification is proposed to increase brightness.
AI.method: The authors show that the normalized second-order coherence function g(2)(τ) of a thermal light source is preserved after amplification, then use amplified thermal light in a LIDAR raster scan of a building at 1.3 km with 2 cm depth resolution.
AI.result: The normalized second-order coherence function g(2)(τ) is preserved after amplification, and amplified thermal light enables a LIDAR raster scan of a building at 1.3 km with 2 cm depth resolution.
AI.conclusion: Optical amplification can boost thermal-light brightness while preserving its second-order coherence, supporting the use of amplified thermal light for kilometer-range LIDAR with centimeter-scale depth resolution.

title: Study of non-uniformity-induced structured spectrum in a tapered optical fiber through stimulated four-wave mixing
summary: Tapered optical fibers offer tunable dispersion and a small mode area, yielding high nonlinearity, which makes them ideal for nonlinear and quantum optics. Because phase-matched four-wave mixing strongly depends on dispersion, the taper diameter becomes a key parameter. For sub-micrometer tapers, identifying the exact diameter is challenging. Here, we show that when seeding with a broad spectrum, stimulated four-wave mixing yields a comb-like spectrum that is directly linked to the overall taper profile opening possibility for non-destructive evaluation of sub-micron taper. Our model based on joint-spectral amplitude includes the phase accumulated over the fiber length.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a non-destructive method for evaluating sub-micrometer tapered optical fibers by seeding a broad spectrum to produce stimulated four-wave-mixing comb-like spectra linked to the taper profile, supported by a joint-spectral-amplitude model that includes phase accumulated along the fiber.
AI.motivation: Tapered optical fibers are attractive for nonlinear and quantum optics because they offer tunable dispersion, small mode area, and high nonlinearity. Phase-matched four-wave mixing depends strongly on dispersion, making taper diameter a key parameter, but identifying the exact diameter of sub-micrometer tapers is challenging.
AI.method: Broad-spectrum seeding is used to generate stimulated four-wave mixing, producing a comb-like spectrum directly linked to the overall taper profile. A model based on joint-spectral amplitude is developed and includes the phase accumulated over the fiber length.
AI.result: Stimulated four-wave mixing with broad-spectrum seeding yields a comb-like spectrum directly linked to the overall taper profile. The joint-spectral-amplitude model incorporates the phase accumulated over the fiber length. Specific quantitative performance metrics are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The approach opens the possibility for non-destructive evaluation of sub-micrometer tapers by linking stimulated four-wave-mixing spectra to the taper profile through a phase-aware joint-spectral-amplitude model.

title: Optical vortex bullets with large angular momenta
comment: 8 pages, 10 figures. To be published in Photonics and Quantum Waves (PQW)
summary: We investigate three-dimensional spatiotemporal optical vortex solitons (light bullets with a toroidal shape) carrying higher-order orbital angular momentum in Kerr media with anomalous group-velocity dispersion and a transversely localized Gaussian profile of the linear refractive index. Stationary vortex bullets with topological charges (winding numbers) $1\leq \ell \leq 4$ are obtained as numerical solutions of the three-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and their existence, structure and stability are systematically analyzed. In terms of atomic Bose-Einstein condensates, these solutions represent matter-wave solitons with embedded vorticity. We examine the dependence of the solution families on the propagation constant, the depth and width of the guiding profile, and $\ell $. It is found that the increase of $\ell $ requires one to use a stronger or wider waveguiding potential to sustain localized states satisfying the Vakhitov-Kolokolov (VK) stability criterion. VK-complying and non-complying branches of vortex-soliton families are separated by a degenerate Townes branch. Direct simulations reveal that, although the guiding profile substantially suppresses the collapse and extends the propagation distance of vortex bullets, their robustness is ultimately limited by azimuthal instabilities, whose growth is enhanced for values of $\ell $. These results demonstrate that engineered refractive-index landscapes significantly enlarge the stability domain of spatiotemporal vortex bullets and provide guidelines for supporting optical bullets carrying large orbital angular momenta.

It analyzes their existence, structure, and stability, including VK criterion branches and azimuthal instability, and shows that engineered guiding landscapes enlarge the stability domain but do not eliminate instability at higher vorticity.

The authors analyze the solution families' dependence on the propagation constant, the depth and width of the guiding profile, and ell, apply the Vakhitov-Kolokolov stability criterion, identify a degenerate Townes branch separating VK-complying and non-complying branches, and perform direct simulations of stability and propagation.

title: Self-Oscillating Photonic Frequency Comb for Sub-THz Local Oscillator Generation in Earth Observation Systems
summary: Earth observation missions rely on microwave and sub-terahertz radiometry for retrieving atmospheric parameters such as temperature, humidity, and cloud properties, with the 183- and 229-GHz spectral regions being particularly relevant. Local-oscillator (LO) generation at these frequencies requires low phase noise and high frequency stability while meeting stringent size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints. Conventional architectures employ dielectric resonator oscillators followed by cascaded frequency-multiplication stages, requiring dedicated generation chains for different frequency bands and increasing hardware complexity. Furthermore, frequency multiplication degrades the phase noise of the generated signal. This work proposes and numerically investigates a reconfigurable self-oscillating microwave photonic architecture for LO generation in Earth observation receivers. Cascaded Mach-Zehnder and phase modulation within an optoelectronic feedback loop generate an optical frequency comb with enhanced higher-order components. A combination of optical filters is used to select the required comb line. First, a conventional bandpass filter with a bandwidth of approximately 10 GHz isolates the spectral region containing the desired component, after which a narrowband dual cavity Bragg grating ring resonator (BGRR) with a bandwidth of approximately 3 MHz provides the final line selection. The selected comb line is then combined with an optical reference derived from the same laser and photodetected to generate the desired millimeter-wave or sub-terahertz signal through optical heterodyning. Numerical simulations are presented for 183- and 229-GHz generation, demonstrating the ability of the same underlying architecture to address multiple LO frequencies by tuning the OEO electrical filter to the appropriate oscillation frequency and selecting the corresponding comb order.

AI.motivation: Earth observation receivers use microwave and sub-terahertz radiometry to retrieve atmospheric temperature, humidity, and cloud properties, especially in the 183- and 229-GHz regions. Local-oscillator generation there requires low phase noise, high frequency stability, and low size, weight, and power. A conventional bandpass filter with approximately 10 GHz bandwidth first isolates the spectral region containing the desired comb component, and a narrowband dual-cavity Bragg grating ring resonator with approximately 3 MHz bandwidth performs final line selection. The selected comb line is combined with an optical reference from the same laser and photodetected to produce millimeter-wave or sub-terahertz signals by optical heterodyning. The same architecture addresses multiple local-oscillator frequencies by tuning the optoelectronic oscillator electrical filter and selecting the corresponding comb order.

Experimental results and measured phase-noise or stability performance are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The numerically investigated reconfigurable microwave photonic architecture can generate local-oscillator signals at both 183 and 229 GHz using a shared optoelectronic-comb approach with dual-stage optical filtering. The abstract supports simulation-based feasibility for multiple frequencies; fabrication, measurement, and experimental validation are not reported.

title: Parameter-efficient neural computing with programmable photonic meshes
summary: Memory capacity and bandwidth are becoming major constraints in neural-network computing, motivating parameter-efficient representations that reduce model storage and data movement. Tensor-network methods already enable substantial compression of neural networks, but their structured operations are often poorly matched to conventional processors optimized for dense linear algebra. Such representations can be implemented in photonic hardware, although this typically requires optical architectures tailored to a particular factorization. Here we propose a different approach based on programmable photonic meshes. Compact electronic parameters determine the interferometer phases, while optical interference produces a dense, generally high-rank transformation. Since the parameterization remains electronic, its dimensionality and structure can be changed without modifying the optical circuit. Numerical experiments in end-to-end training demonstrate that the proposed photonic layers match or outperform strongly compressed tensor-train and brickwork layers, often with fewer trainable parameters. Experiments in parameter-efficient fine-tuning of a language model also show advantages over established digital adapters. The reduced trainable state lowers persistent memory requirements and offers the potential to reduce data movement and bandwidth demands.

AI.tldr: Programmable photonic meshes whose interferometer phases are set by compact electronic parameters can produce dense, high-rank optical transformations while remaining electronically reconfigurable. In numerical experiments, these photonic layers match or outperform strongly compressed tensor-train and brickwork layers, often with fewer trainable parameters, and show advantages over digital adapters in parameter-efficient language-model fine-tuning, reducing trainable state and potentially data movement and bandwidth.
AI.motivation: Neural-network computing is increasingly constrained by memory capacity and bandwidth, motivating parameter-efficient representations that reduce model storage and data movement. Tensor-network methods compress neural networks substantially, but their structured operations are often poorly matched to conventional processors optimized for dense linear algebra. Photonic implementations can realize such representations, but typically require optical architectures tailored to a particular factorization.
AI.method: The paper proposes programmable photonic meshes in which compact electronic parameters determine interferometer phases, while optical interference produces a dense, generally high-rank transformation. Because the parameterization remains electronic, its dimensionality and structure can be changed without modifying the optical circuit. The authors conduct numerical experiments in end-to-end training, comparing the photonic layers with strongly compressed tensor-train and brickwork layers, and experiments in parameter-efficient fine-tuning of a language model, comparing with established digital adapters.
AI.result: Numerical end-to-end training experiments show that the proposed photonic layers match or outperform strongly compressed tensor-train and brickwork layers, often with fewer trainable parameters. In parameter-efficient fine-tuning of a language model, they also show advantages over established digital adapters. The reduced trainable state lowers persistent memory requirements and offers the potential to reduce data movement and bandwidth demands.
AI.conclusion: Programmable photonic meshes provide a flexible, parameter-efficient approach to neural-network layers: compact electronic parameters control optical interference to yield dense high-rank transformations without requiring a factorization-specific optical architecture. The reported results indicate competitive or improved performance relative to compressed tensor-network layers and digital adapters, with lower trainable-state memory and potential bandwidth benefits.

title: Spatiotemporal spherical Gaussian pulses
summary: We describe a class of electromagnetic Gaussian modes with spherical spatiotemporal structure that remains invariant during propagation through anomalously dispersive media. The angular profile of the modes is given by spherical harmonics, whose quantization axis can be freely chosen. As a result, the modes support spatiotemporal orbital angular momentum (OAM) configurations with longitudinal and transverse components set by the orientation of the quantization axis. Superpositions of these modes generalize the familiar solution of a chirped pulse that simultaneously focuses and compresses to arbitrary angular structure. The modes are derived through a series of unitary transformations that map the dispersive paraxial wave equation onto a Schrödinger equation with a 3D isotropic harmonic potential. These transformations facilitate the identification of conserved operators for mixed longitudinal and transverse OAM.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces electromagnetic Gaussian modes with spherical spatiotemporal structure that remain invariant in anomalously dispersive media. Their angular profiles are spherical harmonics with a freely chosen quantization axis, enabling spatiotemporal OAM with longitudinal and transverse components controlled by that axis. The modes are derived by unitary transformations mapping the dispersive paraxial wave equation to a Schrödinger equation with a 3D isotropic harmonic potential, and they yield conserved operators for mixed OAM.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not explicitly state the motivation. The work addresses propagation-invariant spatiotemporal electromagnetic modes in anomalously dispersive media and controllable spatiotemporal OAM, including generalization of the chirped-pulse focusing/compression solution to arbitrary angular structure.
AI.method: The authors derive a class of electromagnetic Gaussian modes whose angular profile is given by spherical harmonics and whose quantization axis can be chosen freely. A series of unitary transformations maps the dispersive paraxial wave equation onto a Schrödinger equation with a 3D isotropic harmonic potential; these transformations are used to identify conserved operators for mixed longitudinal and transverse OAM.

They support spatiotemporal OAM configurations with longitudinal and transverse components determined by the quantization-axis orientation. title: Single-Mode Laser Arrays with Size-Invariant Loss Discrimination
summary: In conventional coupled oscillator lattices and laser arrays, expanding the active volume inevitably causes spectral crowding and degrades spatial uniformity, posing a long-standing barrier to high-power single-mode operation. We uncover a dissipative selection mechanism in sparse star networks that decouples modal selectivity from lattice size constraints. By engineering dissipative auxiliary couplings between a central hub and N peripheral resonators, the system establishes an exact star-Laplacian symmetry. This enforces a target eigenstate that is immune to all lossy channels while maintaining equal amplitude across all main nodes. All competing eigenstates break this symmetry, driving the auxiliary loss and opening a persistent, size-independent modal loss gap that prevents multi-mode competition. Realistic microring simulations validate the robustness of this dark-state isolation under electromagnetic dispersion and mechanism extension to arbitrary arrays is allowed when meets the system's exceptional point. By exploiting graph topology to bypass multi-mode competition, this work establishes a general route toward scalable high-power single-supermode laser arrays and robust state selection in coupled non-Hermitian systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dissipative selection mechanism in sparse star networks that decouples single-mode selectivity from lattice size, using auxiliary lossy couplings to isolate a target eigenstate and suppress competing modes, with microring simulations supporting scalability toward high-power single-supermode laser arrays.
AI.motivation: Conventional coupled oscillator lattices and laser arrays suffer from spectral crowding and degraded spatial uniformity when the active volume is expanded, creating a long-standing barrier to high-power single-mode operation. The work aims to overcome multi-mode competition without being constrained by lattice size.
AI.method: The authors engineer dissipative auxiliary couplings between a central hub and N peripheral resonators to establish an exact star-Laplacian symmetry. This symmetry enforces a target eigenstate that is immune to all lossy channels and has equal amplitude across all main nodes, while all competing eigenstates break the symmetry, drive auxiliary loss, and open a persistent, size-independent modal loss gap. Realistic microring simulations are used to test robustness under electromagnetic dispersion, and extension to arbitrary arrays is considered when the system's exceptional point condition is met.
AI.result: The proposed star-network configuration yields dark-state isolation of the target eigenstate and a size-independent modal loss gap that prevents multi-mode competition. Microring simulations validate the robustness of this isolation under electromagnetic dispersion. The abstract does not provide quantitative performance metrics or experimental results.

title: Measuring the Quantum Phase of Multiphoton Systems
summary: The quantum phase of a multiparticle system has remained a long-standing mystery in quantum physics. The absence of a phase operator that faithfully represents this physical quantity has prevented the formulation of a meaningful uncertainty relation with particle number. Here, we resolve this problem by measuring, for the first time, the quantum phase of multiparticle systems containing up to fifteen particles. We achieve this through a new quantum state tomography scheme that combines homodyne interferometry with photon-number-resolving detection. This approach enables us to reconstruct complementary photon-number and phase representations and establish the corresponding number-phase uncertainty relation. Our measurements further provide access to the mutually unbiased basis of a multiparticle system, a fundamental resource for multiparticle quantum information processing. Furthermore, we report the spatially resolved characterization of the quantum phase. These results provide an operational framework for measuring quantum phase in multiparticle systems, with implications for fundamental quantum physics and scalable multiparticle quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the first measurement of the quantum phase of multiparticle systems with up to fifteen particles using quantum state tomography that combines homodyne interferometry and photon-number-resolving detection, enabling number-phase uncertainty relations, mutually unbiased basis access, and spatially resolved phase characterization.
AI.motivation: The quantum phase of multiparticle systems has remained a long-standing mystery, and the absence of a phase operator that faithfully represents this quantity has prevented a meaningful uncertainty relation with particle number from being formulated.
AI.method: The authors perform quantum phase measurement for multiparticle systems containing up to fifteen particles using a new quantum state tomography scheme combining homodyne interferometry with photon-number-resolving detection, reconstructing complementary photon-number and phase representations; they also characterize the spatially resolved quantum phase.
AI.result: The authors measure the quantum phase of multiparticle systems for the first time, establish the corresponding number-phase uncertainty relation, and gain access to the mutually unbiased basis of a multiparticle system; they further report spatially resolved characterization of the quantum phase.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an operational framework for measuring quantum phase in multiparticle systems, with implications for fundamental quantum physics and scalable multiparticle quantum technologies.

title: Time-resolved transient absorption spectroscopy with quantum light
summary: We present a fully quantum theory of time-resolved transient absorption spectroscopy, providing a general framework for describing the linear response of a nonequilibrium target to quantum probe fields beyond the semiclassical approximation. We elucidate how quantum correlations between probe-field frequency modes couple to coherences in the target and derive a simple expression for computing the resulting spectroscopic signals. We identify conditions under which quantum light can modify transient absorption spectra beyond the limits achievable with classical fields. Our work establishes a theoretical foundation for exploiting quantum light in ultrafast spectroscopy and suggests new routes for resolving dynamics in matter on timescales shorter than the duration of the probe pulse.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a fully quantum theory of time-resolved transient absorption spectroscopy for nonequilibrium targets probed by quantum fields beyond the semiclassical approximation, showing how probe-field quantum correlations affect spectroscopic signals and when quantum light can outperform classical fields.

title: Demonstration of continuous non-invasive monitoring of plant metabolism using mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy
summary: Life is a rhythmic process driven by cellular and physiological mechanisms that allow plants to respond and adapt to their environment. In addition to natural fluctuations, plants are increasingly exposed to environmental stresses, mainly caused by climate change and anthropogenic pollution. Multiple approaches across different biological scales (gene, cell, metabolite, and physiology) have shed light on acclimation mechanisms but generally lack sufficient temporal resolution. Establishing a non-invasive and high-temporal-resolution monitoring method to measure plant activity across different conditions is therefore needed to fully assess how plant metabolism changes under stress. Here, we established a novel approach to perform continuous and non-invasive mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy on vascular plants, with the aim of identifying and monitoring the chemical composition of peripheral tissues, including sap, over periods ranging from a few minutes to several months. We describe an experimental setup, the physics underlying its operation, and present a multi-day acquisition. Compared with controls, data enabled to identify a diurnal pattern, with peaks of approximately equal duration, that recurred consistently over the experiment. Estimations of the impact of instrumental and environmental fluctuations indicate that the signal amplitude and trends cannot be explained by instrumental drifts. The experiment thus demonstrated the detection of a signal associated with plant physiological activity. While its origins remain to be clarified, this preliminary experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the measurements and provides a basis for future developments.

title: A GRACE Interatomic Potential for W--Ta Systems: Application to Ta Segregation and Pinning of Shear-Coupled Grain-Boundary Migration
summary:
Tungsten-tantalum alloys are promising plasma-facing materials for fusion reactors, but simulations of their coupled defect, mechanical, and microstructural evolution require an interatomic potential that remains accurate across diverse atomic environments. We develop a transferable W-Ta potential within the GRaph Atomic Cluster Expansion (GRACE) framework. The primary training dataset was generated automatically by maximizing information entropy in an atomically relevant feature space, avoiding manual enumeration of the structures and processes required for specific downstream applications. Extensive validation demonstrates a consistent description of unary and binary phase stability, elasticity, phonons, high-pressure response, surfaces, point defects, dislocation energetics, transformation pathways, alloy thermodynamics, and melting behavior.
